claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) describes Schwab's operating efficiency, 'coupled with scale' and shared infrastructure across businesses, as creating a cost advantage that lets it price competitively while profitably serving clients of various sizes across multiple channels. It also lists brand and reputation as enabling Schwab to attract clients, and service culture as raising the likelihood that clients refer others.
The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says Schwab was founded to give individual investors access to the markets at a highly competitive cost.

On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), CEO Rick Wurster said Schwab's 'sheer scale, combined with efficiency efforts' keeps cost-to-serve low and lets it invest in client capabilities. He also said that, with nearly $12 trillion in assets and more than 46 million client accounts, doing more for existing clients is as important a growth source as acquiring new clients.

The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) states that management works to couple Schwab's scale and resources with ongoing expense discipline to keep costs low and products affordable. The 10-Q calls this part of its 'no trade-offs' approach.

In the 3Q26 deck (published 2026-10-15), Schwab's 'Keep Cost to Serve Low' page lists a goal to 'leverage our scale to maintain a structural cost advantage while continuing to invest in growth'. The page shows 90% of accounts opened digitally, 82% first call resolution and a 30-second average speed to answer.

Results Schwab cites for 2025: the 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) reports 4.7 million new brokerage accounts (up 13%), core net new assets of $519.4 billion (up 42%, a 5.1% organic growth rate) and 38.5 million active brokerage accounts.

Results Schwab cites for 2026: the 3Q26 press release (2026-10-15) reports 1.2 million new brokerage accounts and $190.4 billion of core net new assets, up 38% versus 3Q25. It also reports 48.6 million total client accounts.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Wurster said Schwab is investing for future client growth in more branches in local communities, more financial consultants, 'strategic marketing and advertising' (including adapting marketing to the influence of LLMs), an RIA support ecosystem and its workplace clients. Per management, acquisition at scale is paired with continued spending, not only low cost.

On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management said 33% of new-to-firm retail households were under age 30 and more than 50% were under 40. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), Wurster said 1.9 million new retail households came to Schwab in 2025, and the average new-to-firm retail client is in their 30s.

Workplace: Schwab's investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) says Workplace Services introduces new clients to Retail and Advisor Services. It shows ~400K new-to-firm households introduced by Workplace, ~50% of retirement rollovers retained by Schwab, and ~27% of workplace households using additional Schwab products and solutions.

Workplace: on the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management described a 'multiyear effort to introduce even more workplace clients to our investing and wealth management capabilities'. Schwab's August 2026 monthly report cites 5.9 million workplace plan participant accounts.

Retail: on the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster said clients with a financial consultant relationship bring in more than two times the net new assets, and are more engaged in managed investing and banking, than clients without one. The 10-K (2026-02-25) describes a multichannel service model (online, mobile, phone, branch) and entry products such as Schwab Stock Slices and the Schwab Starter Kit.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2025-06-30 [IR]; SCHW 10-K - Investor Services segment 2025-12-31 [filing]

claims.text: Retail digital: Schwab's 3Q26 deck (2026-10-15) shows 90% of accounts opened digitally. The 3Q26 release says Schwab introduced 'Charley', an AI-powered assistant for U.S. retail clients.

Advisor Services: on the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster said Schwab launched Advisor ProDirect, a fee-based, membership-driven offer designed to support independence for new RIAs. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), he said Schwab attracts net new assets from new and existing advisors of all sizes. The 3Q26 release (2026-10-15) says Schwab partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2025-06-30 [IR]; SCHW transcript 2025-12-31 [IR]; SCHW press 2026-09-30 [filing]

claims.text: Acquisition integration (Ameritrade): on the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management said it captured 100% of the Ameritrade run-rate expense synergies in 2024. On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster called it the most consequential integration in the industry's history. He said Ameritrade clients moved from losing assets to stable and then growing, and that he expects Ameritrade to become a more meaningful part of net new assets.

Acquisition integration (Forge): the 1Q26 release (2026-04-16) says Schwab closed the Forge Global acquisition in early March 2026. On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Wurster said Forge will give clients access to pre-IPO shares, to be rolled out over time. He also described a private issuer Equity Services offer that combines the workplace business with Qapita technology and transitions to Schwab's public stock plan services.

claims.text: On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), CFO Sharon Yeshaya described "channel migration": Workplace assets that begin in Workplace and move into the advisor-led channel. She said that since 2020, $300 billion had come from Workplace and moved into advisor-led.

On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), Yeshaya said Morgan Stanley has an exclusive partnership with Carta, under which Carta will refer private companies and their stock plans to Morgan Stanley as they go public. She said the firm is committed to a seamless experience for those clients.

On the 1Q25 call (April 2025), Yeshaya cited an incremental $20 billion that quarter migrating to the advisor-led channel from workplace. She said this added to the roughly $300 billion accumulated from workplace since the channel was expanded in 2020.

On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Yeshaya said 70% of the flows that originate from workplace are net new assets to the firm. She also said the firm used to say about $16 billion per year originated from workplace and was running ahead of that. She said advisor-led flows come from existing advisors, recruits and the origination of workplace.

On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), Yeshaya said the $300 billion workplace-migration figure had been accompanied by about $60 billion of migration per year. She said that three quarters into the year the firm was already exceeding that on a full-year basis. She also described LeadIQ, an AI-powered lead distribution platform that matches workplace and self-directed relationships with financial advisors.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), a company representative said advisor-led assets originating from workplace and E*TRADE relationships grew to a record $99 billion for the full year, compared with historical averages of around $60 billion per year. CEO Ted Pick said the three channels (financial advisors, Workplace, E*TRADE) together make up the firm's "strategic client acquisition model".

The January 2026 strategic update deck defines "Advisor-Led Flows from Workplace and E*TRADE" as assets brought into advisor-led relationships where the initial account was workplace or self-directed. The deck's figures are averaged over 2020 to 2024.

On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Yeshaya said that since 2020 the firm had generated over $400 billion of new adviser-led assets from relationships that originated in Workplace or E*TRADE. She said that, including Workplace assets on the platform before the E*TRADE acquisition, adviser-led assets sourced from Workplace and E*TRADE exceed $1.2 trillion, roughly 20% of $5.8 trillion of adviser-led assets. She described a first step of retaining vested assets (greater retention that quarter, which translated into NNA), followed by channel migration as Workplace assets seek advice.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Yeshaya said new accounts and existing clients both contribute, and it is hard to say exactly where each lands. She said that for those without an advice-based relationship, "we're working on that referral model". She said this can begin as early as financial education and can include 401(k) assets that are not IPO-specific. Pick said growth led by workplace relationships "reflects a cornerstone of our client acquisition funnel".

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Pick said the firm has an integrated funnel of self-directed, a "differentiated workplace offering that continues to expand and source new relationships", and the financial adviser relationship. Yeshaya said that as IPOs come to market, "real relationships, adviser-led relationships" are being built, and described this as the top part of the funnel.

The 10-K for 2025 (published February 2026) reports the workplace channel at December 31, 2025: stock plan unvested assets of $534 billion (versus $475 billion at the end of 2024) and 6.5 million participants (versus 6.6 million). The 10-K says the participant count declined slightly primarily because of the disposition of the EMEA stock plan business.

The 1Q26 10-Q (May 2026) reports stock plan unvested public assets of $475 billion and stock plan participants of 6.6 million at March 31, 2026 (December 31, 2025: $534 billion and 6.5 million). The 2Q26 10-Q (August 2026) reports $658 billion and 6.6 million at June 30, 2026. The 3Q26 supplement (October 2026) reports stock plan unvested public assets of $638 billion.

claims.text: For scale at the start of the build-out, the 4Q20 supplement (January 2021) showed 4,885 thousand workplace participants and $435 billion of workplace unvested assets at December 31, 2020.

The 2Q26 10-Q (August 2026) says net new assets of $148 billion for the quarter included just over half in inflows related to IPOs of certain clients in the Workplace channel. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Yeshaya said stock plan IPO flows were just over half of NNA, and that this more than offset seasonal taxes.

claims.text: The 3Q26 supplement (October 2026) shows total Wealth Management net new assets of $232.4 billion and fee-based asset flows of $80.5 billion. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Yeshaya said fee-based flows of $80 billion had nearly half coming from a corporate retirement mandate. She said the firm is expanding its retirement capabilities and deepening engagement with plan participants.
claims.source_label: MS supplement - Wealth Management segment 2026-09-30, p.8 [IR]; MS transcript 2026-09-30 [IR]

claims.text: On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Yeshaya said that since acquiring E*TRADE and expanding the workplace offering 6 years ago, the firm has added over $2 trillion of net new assets, and now has $8.4 trillion in client assets and nearly 21 million relationships. This figure is for the whole funnel, not workplace alone.

On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), Yeshaya said that as IPOs come to market, people bring their assets to Morgan Stanley. She said they drop into self-directed accounts but also move directly into advisor-led accounts, and that workplace is bringing in assets into NNA and directly into fee-based flows.

The January 2026 strategic update deck lays out offerings by client stage. For corporates, founders and employees it lists financial wellness and employee benefits, founders wealth strategies, private shares trading and lending, IPO execution and support services, full-service wealth advice and asset allocation, and family office, trust and estate solutions. Under "Access to Capital" it lists MS at Work cap table management, cash management solutions, private capital markets, tenders, financing and IPO, and MS at Work stock plan and 401k.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Yeshaya said the referral model for participants without an advice relationship can begin at the financial education stage and with 401(k) assets. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), she said that as fund lockups expire, assets are distributed to underlying investors into individual accounts, which is another place the funnel moves into an advice-based relationship.

On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), the CFO cited an expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets as part of investing in the platform. The 4Q24 call (January 2025) described Carta as referring private companies' stock plans to Morgan Stanley as they approach going public.

The 2025 10-K describes Wealth Management's offering as including workplace services such as stock plan administration, securities-based lending, residential and commercial real estate loans, banking, cash management and retirement plan services. On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Yeshaya said household lending penetration grew across the advisor-led channel.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), a Wolfe Research analyst asked about press coverage of smaller RIAs using more aggressive pricing to compete for workplace business and about sustaining client conversion rates. Yeshaya replied that "it's always been a competitive business". She said the firm keeps adding capabilities, options and a greater lens of investment, and that it starts with corporate coverage, using the Integrated Firm to build corporate relationships at the top of the funnel.

The 2025 10-K (February 2026) says Morgan Stanley's ability to compete across channels (advisor led, workplace and digital direct) is affected by multiple factors. These include brand and reputation, the breadth, depth and pricing of product offerings, and technology supporting evolving client needs.

The 4Q24 call (January 2025) named headwinds for workplace: Yeshaya said the firm had not been in a cycle with many monetization events, and that participant counts were affected by sold stock plan businesses in Europe and Asia and by headcount reductions or acquisitions at plan companies. On the 1Q25 call (April 2025), she said workplace is "a little bit less in our control", citing stock grants and the possibility of fewer IPO events.

The 2Q26 10-Q (August 2026) says NNA is influenced by factors including capital market and corporate activities that affect assets in certain client channels, and large idiosyncratic inflows and outflows. It adds that "the growth rate of our NNA may be impacted" should these factors continue.

On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), Pick said the KPIs are whether the firm is increasing the TAM of relationships across the financial advisory lever, Workplace and self-directed, and fee-based flows. The January 2026 strategic update deck lists firmwide goals of a 30% WM pre-tax margin, client assets of $10 trillion+, ROTCE of 20% and an efficiency ratio of 70%.

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Pick said NNA "will ebb and flow in a given quarter". He said that, beyond IPO events, the firm's presence with many private companies leads it to believe "this cycle has many years to come". Yeshaya said she expects pretax margin to expand over time with scale, and that the firm intends to invest over the long term rather than manage the margin quarter by quarter.

claims.text: The FY2025 10-K (period 2025-09-30, published 2025-11-25) states that Raymond James offers multiple affiliation options, which it calls AdvisorChoice®. Financial advisors primarily affiliate directly as employees or independent contractors, or as employees of third-party RIAs and broker-dealers that the firm serves through its RIA and Custody Services (RCS) division.

The 2025 10-K describes employee advisors as working in a traditional branch supported by local management and administrative staff, serving predominantly retail clients. Independent contractor advisors are generally responsible for all their direct costs. They may affiliate directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in the Financial Institutions Division. The 10-K says the independent contractor options are designed to let advisors use as much or as little of the firm's support as they determine they need.

The 2025 10-K reports 8,943 advisors as of September 30, 2025: 3,878 employees and 5,065 independent contractors. The prior-year figures were 3,826 employees and 4,961 independent contractors (8,787 total).

The Investor Day deck (published 2025-06-05) lays out the AdvisorChoice spectrum in three groups. Employee: Employee Advisor (RJA) and Advisor Select. Independent Contractor: Independent Advisor (ICD), Banks and Credit Unions, and IAR (Corporate RIA). RIA & Custody Services is the third group. The slide title says the spectrum services the largest addressable market in the industry.

The affiliation options recruiting page (content as of 2026-04-21) lists five options under AdvisorChoice®: Traditional Employee, Advisor Select, Independent Contractor, Bank & Credit Union, and Corporate RIA. The page's comparison table adds RIA & Custody Services. It lists entry qualifications for each: Traditional Employee needs a minimum of 5 years of experience. Advisor Select needs 3 years and $3.5 million or higher in annual branch fees and commission revenue. Independent Contractor needs 3 years and a minimum T12 of $150,000 to join an existing branch or $400,000 to open a new one. Bank & Credit Union needs 3 years and $250,000 in production. Corporate RIA needs 3 years and $50 million in assets under advisement.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: The same page (content as of 2026-04-21) sets RCS entry requirements: $100 million or more in assets to establish a new RIA, a minimum of $30 million to plug in an existing RIA, and $1 billion or more in assets under management for introducing broker/dealers. It says that under RCS you are responsible for compliance. Employee, Advisor Select, and Bank & Credit Union advisors get compliance support from a branch manager and the home office. Independent Contractor and Corporate RIA advisors get it from a divisional team and the home office.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-04-21 [IR]

claims.text: The Advisor Select page (content as of 2026-03-11) describes it as an employee affiliation option for established advisors. It gives the benefits of the employee channel, with independence to create their own branch. The advisor chooses a location, builds out the office and runs the branch's P&L to earn a higher rate on production.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-03-11 [IR]

claims.text: The Independent Advisor page (content as of 2026-05-19) describes independent contractor advisors as supported by a full-service, self-clearing NYSE-member broker/dealer. It also describes a Corporate RIA affiliation model, in which fee-based advisors get the RIA experience while the firm streamlines many of its burdens.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-05-19 [IR]

claims.text: The RCS page (content as of 2026-07-12) describes RCS as giving independent RIAs strategic, financial and administrative control, free from retail conflict, using as much or as little of the firm's support as they need. Listed support includes a dedicated service associate, transitions management, an integrated technology platform that can incorporate third-party applications, marketing, practice management, succession planning and acquisition, and RCS business-development help to recruit advisors.
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-07-12 [IR]

claims.text: The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-31 (published 2026-05-06) reports PCG AUA associated with RCS firms of $228.2 billion at March 31, 2026, versus $185.6 billion at March 31, 2025. Of the $228.2 billion, $199.1 billion was in fee-based accounts. The filing says RCS growth is partly due to transfers into RCS from the firm's other advisor channels. It does not expect these transfers to significantly impact results of operations.

On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), CEO Paul Shoukry said advisors differ in how they spend their time. Some want close to 100% of their time on building books and serving clients, which he said aligns more with the employee option. Others also want to run a business, including building a team, paying for benefits, real estate and legal matters.

The 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says employee advisors' compensation primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate, and they participate in the firm's employee benefit plans. Independent contractor advisors pay all their direct costs and receive a higher payout percentage than employee advisors.

Raymond James's affiliation options page (content as of 2026-04-21) lists these headline payouts. Traditional Employee: up to 50% payout plus employee benefits. Advisor Select: 70-80% gross payout plus employee benefits. Independent Contractor: 81% to 90% payout, with benefits built through third-party partnerships. Corporate RIA: 81% to 90% payout. Bank & Credit Union: a competitive compensation package from the financial institution in partnership with Raymond James. RIA & Custody Services: compensation is determined by the advisor's RIA or broker/dealer, who create their own benefits package.

claims.text: On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), CEO Shoukry said independent payouts are higher because independent advisors cover their own overhead (real estate, health insurance, and so on). He said much more of the last year's recruiting came from the independent side, creating a mix shift. He added that the employee side has tiered payout systems, so advisors move up the payout grid as production increases. In a separate answer he tied the mix shift to the comp ratio more than to margin.

The 2025 10-K (Item 7) says that in PCG the firm generally charges either asset-based fees (shown in 'Asset management and related administrative fees') or sales commissions (shown in 'Brokerage revenues'). It also earns revenue from distribution and related services on funds, annuities and insurance products. These revenues are typically correlated with PCG client AUA and U.S. equity markets. Fee-based account fees are mostly billed on beginning-of-quarter balances.

The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-31 (published 2026-05-06) says revenue from fee-based AUA in PCG is shared between PCG and the Asset Management segment. Asset Management receives a higher portion for accounts in managed programs, because it performs portfolio management as well as administrative services. For RCS firms, the same 10-Q says revenues on RCS assets are included in PCG 'Account and service fees'.

On the fiscal 4Q24 call (published 2024-10-23), then-CEO Paul Reilly said that for the RIA custody business the firm 'really get[s] an asset fee'. He said the firm's net basis points on those assets are lower, but RCS has higher margins by the way RIA custody is measured. He explained there are fewer supervision and compliance requirements: RIAs' clients are the RIAs' clients, not Raymond James's. He said this detail had not been disclosed and might be shown at a future analyst day.

On the fiscal 1Q25 call (published 2025-01-29), Shoukry said transition assistance for recruited advisors is amortized over time. He said revenue has been growing with the S&P 500 and recruiting (17% for fee-based assets year over year), while the transition assistance amortization is not growing that fast. He saw a possible modest scale benefit, while noting that the firm is still recruiting heavily so transition assistance will keep growing.

The earnings press release for the period ended 2025-12-31 (published 2026-01-28) defines 'PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation' as cash and equity awards issued for recruiting, as retention for existing advisors, or in conjunction with acquisitions. These awards are expensed over the requisite service period, typically between 5 and 10 years.

claims.text: Management on the fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28) said it broke out retention and transition assistance expense for the first time because recruiting over the prior 12 months, advisors with $460 million at prior firms, is equivalent to a decent-sized acquisition. Shoukry said the firm prefers to recruit one by one because the advisors are a good cultural fit, and 100% of transition assistance goes to retention rather than to a seller. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22) he repeated this and said recruiting yields 'very good returns'.

Management ties retention to growth. The 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says domestic financial advisor retention remained very strong for the year ended September 30, 2025. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), Shoukry said the firm ended the fiscal year with a record number of financial advisors, 2% higher than the prior year. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), he credited 'adviser choice' for 7% annualized net new assets in the first half of the year, from both recruiting and retention. On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), he cited $75 billion of net new assets so far that fiscal year, up 119% from a record the prior year. claims.text: On the fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23), Shoukry said that once an advisor affiliates there is a lag, which could be three, six or nine months, before assets show up in net new assets. He also said the firm was still seeing pressure on its existing advisor base from private equity-backed roll-ups, which compete 'with big checks'.

Headwinds the firm names: the 2025 10-K (Item 1A, published 2025-11-25) cites an industry-wide trend of advisors leaving traditional firms, including to independent RIAs, some backed by private equity, which has made recruiting highly competitive. It says other firms offer guaranteed contracts and upfront payments, and that recruiting incentives raise the firm's costs. It also says advisors may leave to unaffiliated RIAs and retiring advisors without a successor may sell their practices to third parties. Management mitigates this through succession planning and by providing advisors a broad range of services and resources.

Specific departures management has flagged. On the fiscal 4Q24 call (published 2024-10-23), Reilly said several OSJ relationships in the independent contractor division were leaving the platform, with roughly $3 billion of AUA leaving in the quarter and approximately $5 billion more expected in early fiscal 2025. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), Shoukry said a platform of about $2.7 billion of assets would be lost to bank M&A the next quarter.
The Investor Day deck (published 2025-06-05) lists recruiting themes: collaborative recruiting across channels, West Coast and Northeast focus, and a next-gen advisor strategy.

The fiscal 2Q26 press release (published 2026-04-22) quotes Shoukry saying that financial advisor recruiting activity across all affiliation options remains robust. The fiscal 3Q26 release (published 2026-07-22) cites robust recruiting as supporting momentum entering the fiscal fourth quarter.

Management describes a 'best-of-both-worlds' value proposition: an advisor and client-focused culture combined with leading technology and solutions. On the fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23) it said this resonates with advisors across all affiliation options, and that its strong balance sheet and commitment to independence are increasingly a differentiator. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22) Shoukry said many competitors 'compete with the largest check', and that many are looking for an exit in three to five years or even less. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22) and fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), management said advisors 'do not have to choose between culture and capabilities'.

claims.text: How it earns - Schwab: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) states that Schwab's largest sources of net revenues are net interest revenue, asset management and administration fees, trading revenue, and bank deposit account fees. Net interest revenue is the difference between interest generated on interest-earning assets and interest paid on funding sources. Schwab's primary funding source is uninvested client cash held on its balance sheet.

How it earns - Schwab: The 2025 10-K describes bank deposit account fees as revenue from sweeping uninvested client cash off-balance sheet to accounts at the TD Depository Institutions. Schwab provides marketing, recordkeeping and support services in exchange. The revenues are based on floating and fixed yields elected by the Company, less interest paid to clients and other fees.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-08), Schwab says it sets the rates paid on certain brokerage client cash balances and bank deposits and the rates charged on certain margin and bank loans. It also controls the composition of its investment securities. It says this lets it take actions to manage its net interest spread, depending on competitive factors and market conditions.

How it earns - Schwab: The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-08) says Schwab earns mutual fund and ETF service fees and asset management fees based on daily balances of certain client assets. Changes in equity valuations therefore directly affect fee revenue.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 2Q26 results release (published 2026-07-21), Schwab reported net interest margin of 3.00% and client transactional sweep cash of $485.7 billion. Asset management and administration fees grew 16% year-over-year to $1.8 billion. Trading revenue was $1.2 billion, up 28% year-over-year.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 3Q26 results release (published 2026-10-15), Schwab reported net interest margin of 3.04% and client transactional sweep cash of $492.8 billion. Asset management and administration fees grew 14% year-over-year to $1.9 billion. Trading revenue was $1.2 billion, up 16% year-over-year.

How it earns - Morgan Stanley: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) says Wealth Management asset management revenues relate to advisory services on fee-based assets, account service and administration, and distribution of products. They are generally based on the net asset value of the account in which a client is invested.

How it earns - Morgan Stanley: On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-15), the CFO cited Wealth Management asset management revenues of $5.3 billion and transactional revenues of $1.2 billion. She said deposits grew sequentially to $436 billion and net interest income increased to $2.3 billion. She said NII outperformed on higher-than-expected sweep balances and strong loan growth.

How it earns - Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) shows 2025 total revenue of $17,897 million. Asset-based fees were $14,138 million (79%), account and activity fees $747 million (4%), trade revenue $1,832 million (10%), interest and dividends $1,062 million (6%), and other revenue, net $118 million (1%). Asset-based fees include advisory programs fees, service fees and other asset-based fees.

How it earns - Edward Jones: The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-07) says advisory program fees are based on the average daily market value of client assets in the program. Trade revenue is commissions and principal transactions. Net interest and dividends revenue is a separate category.

How it earns - Merrill: The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-07-31) says Merrill Wealth Management revenue of $5.7 billion increased 16 percent. It attributes this primarily to higher asset management fees (higher market valuations and positive AUM flows) and higher brokerage fees from increased transactional volume.

How it earns - Raymond James: The FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says the Private Client Group generally charges either asset-based fees or sales commissions. It also earns servicing fees from product companies and from banks to which it sweeps client cash through RJBDP, its multi-bank sweep program.

How it earns - Raymond James: The fiscal 3Q26 release (published 2026-07-22) says PCG asset management and related administrative fees grew 19% to $1.73 billion, mainly on market appreciation and net inflows into fee-based accounts. Pre-tax income was affected by lower interest rates. Total clients' domestic cash sweep and Enhanced Savings Program balances were $58.8 billion.

claims.text: What drives it - Schwab: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says a reduction in clients' allocation to cash, a change in how that cash is allocated, or a transfer of cash away would likely reduce its income. It cites 2022-2023, when clients moved from sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives at Schwab and Schwab used higher-cost funding that hurt net income.

It says price competition such as reduced commissions or higher deposit rates could affect results.

He said clients in Schwab Wealth Advisory generate 3x the ROCA of retail clients. He framed the combination as a way to "diversify our economics over the long term."

claims.text: Position: personalization at scale, with the human relationship kept. Capgemini's World Wealth Report (published 2026-06-03) says the future of wealth management "will be defined by personalization at scale, underpinned by empathetic advisory relationships." It says life transitions, liquidity events and behavioral signals will increasingly decide when and how firms interact with clients, replacing calendar-driven review cycles with relevance-driven ones.

Position: trusted personal relationships stay central, helped by technology. On the 2Q26 earnings call (July 2026), Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry said "the real value in this business has always been and always will be true personal relationships." He said that cannot be replicated by AI or technology "but it will be helped by AI and technology." He said the firm will keep investing in people, platforms and capabilities to help advisors deliver more holistic and personalized advice.

Position: advice stays a people business. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CEO said that even if the technology is world-class, clients want to make decisions with their financial advisers based on the complexity of their own needs. He said technology can "do a lot of the early work."

Position: digital-first expectations and more acceptance of virtual advisor relationships. A Wealthtender advisor-search study (published 2025-08-13) says consumers now expect digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice. Based on its data, it anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches. It also anticipates faster response expectations and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.

Position: competitive pressure from AI and robo-advice is reshaping delivery. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the industry has more firms providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences, including AI and lower-cost computer-based "robo-advice." It says this has led, and is expected to keep leading, to significant investments in financial advisors, technology infrastructure, digital initiatives and data-powered tools. It also names changing client expectations and demographics, and generational wealth transfer, as risks to its ability to adapt its business model.

Position: advice-led, fee-based relationships as the destination for clients. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CFO said clients either come in directly as fee-based accounts or migrate over time from self-directed. She said a little over 20% of all adviser-led flows are fee-based flows and that this "still holds, if not growing."

Position: AI augments advisors rather than replacing them. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Raymond James CEO Shoukry said the firm tells advisors: "AI will not replace advisers. Advisers who use AI will replace advisers who do not use AI." He said administrative time saved lets advisors spend more time on personal relationships. He said management believes the long-term ROI will exceed the cost of using AI.

Position: AI as "enhanced intelligence." On the 3Q25 call (published 2025-10-15), Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said the firm views AI as "enhanced intelligence, not an artificial intelligence," with teammates critical to delivering services. In the 2Q25 call (published 2025-07-16) he said AI helps relationship managers and advisors search and summarize information to prepare personalized planning and pitches.

Position: agentic AI could free up large amounts of advisor time. Deloitte (published 2026-05-20) says advisers spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work, leaving 30% for building client relationships. Its Center for Financial Services predicts adviser productivity uplift of roughly 30% to 100% by 2032. It says this could free between 25% and 50% of adviser time and potentially shift the issue from adviser scarcity to adviser capability.

Position: AI will transform advice, but most expect task automation. Accenture's survey (published 2025-06-23) found 97% say AI will have a transformative effect on the future of financial advice to a moderate or great extent in the next three years. 55% say AI will be most helpful in eliminating administrative tasks, identifying next best action opportunities, and automating marketing and client contact.

Position: AI will replace tasks, not the advisor, in core segments, though lower-touch models and younger clients may be different. McKinsey (published 2026-04-08) says the replacement thesis is "mostly false" for core advice segments, where nearly 80 percent of affluent households still prefer a human relationship. It says an AI takeover "might indeed be possible" for standardized, lower-touch service models and for younger clients, who are increasingly comfortable with AI-only interfaces.

Position: AI opens new distribution and more personal service. At Schwab on the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-16), CEO Rick Wurster said "AI opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to-person relationship." Schwab's 3Q26 release (published 2026-10-15) says it introduced Charley, an AI-powered assistant giving U.S. retail clients conversational access to Schwab's tools and insights. It also partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.

Position: client comfort with AI is highest for monitoring and administrative tasks. A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13, data snapshot from July 2025) found 77% comfortable with AI monitoring accounts for unusual activity. 74% were comfortable with AI analyzing market data to inform recommendations, and 74% with AI drafting routine client communications. The study says comfort with AI is lower for autonomous decision-making.

Position: AI and digital tools carry risks the firms themselves name. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says that as it deploys new digital tools and client-facing technologies, its exposure to fraud risk is expected to increase. It also says use of AI may expose the firm to additional information security, legal and regulatory risk. The Raymond James FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says inadequate AI practices could produce inaccurate or biased output, and says AI could raise security and privacy risks.

Position: advisors will be expected to deliver more holistic and bespoke advice. On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), Raymond James CEO Shoukry said advisors "have been expected and will continue to be expected to provide more holistic and bespoke financial advice." He said this will require the firm to provide technology, where AI can help. Schwab's 2026 investor-day deck (published 2026-05-14) lists "growing demand for holistic advice" and "rising investor expectations for sophisticated, personalized solutions."

Position: demand for holistic advice is rising. McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) reports the share of investors seeking more holistic advice grew from 29 percent in 2018 to 52 percent in 2023. Capgemini (published 2026-06-03) reports 47% of HNWIs will consolidate more wealth with wealth management firms that provide integrated access to specialists. A Barclays commercial director quoted there says future relationship managers will need to move from reactive, product-centric interactions toward more intentional, coordinated engagement.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-02-10, p.2 [research]; Research research 2026-06-03, p.30 [research]

claims.text: Position: next-generation clients want holistic planning and fee transparency. Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) says wealthy Gen X, Y and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning and life goal achievement. These households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management.

Position: clients will pay for human advice, and fee rates have held steady. McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) says almost 80 percent of surveyed affluent households would rather pay a premium of 50 basis points or more for human advice than use a customized digital advice service priced at about ten basis points. It cites PriceMetrix by McKinsey showing fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships averaging approximately 104 basis points since 2019, after compression from 2013 to 2018.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-02-10, p.2 [research]; Research research 2025-02-10, p.3 [research]

claims.text: Position: fee-based advice has room to grow at self-directed firms. On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-21), Schwab CEO Wurster said only 5% of Schwab retail households are in a fee-based advice solution and 31% of Schwab clients said they are willing to pay for advice. Cerulli (published 2026-04-09) says even among investors with under $100,000 in financial assets, just 34% say they are not willing to pay for advice. It says self-directed platforms need a path of least resistance from self-directed to advised.

Position: advisor roles may shift toward capability and relationships, and affiliation models are uncertain. Deloitte (published 2026-05-20) says AI could potentially shift the issue from adviser scarcity to adviser capability. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Raymond James's CEO said that whether AI could create convergence among affiliation options is a "potentially" and "interesting to see how that kind of evolves over time" question.

Edward Jones's own stated direction (2025 10-K, published 2026-03-13): the firm describes investing in initiatives such as Financial Planning Services, where clients receive a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities. It also describes targeting High Net Worth clients, Workplace, and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. The 10-K says it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives.

Position: automation paired with professional oversight within advisor-led relationships. Merrill's press release (2026-09-15) announced Tax Efficient Transition and Dollar Cost Averaging services in its Investment Advisory Program. The release says they combine automation with professional portfolio oversight to help advisors implement personalized investment strategies at scale. Clients are directed to speak with their Merrill advisor about eligibility.

Position: advice tiered by client wealth segment. At its November 2025 investor day (published 2025-11-05), Bank of America's deck described a Wealth Continuum. It labels Mass Market (<$500K) as "investment tools" with a "predominantly digital experience." It labels Mass Affluent ($500K-$1MM) as "goals-based advice" with "guidance delivered at scale." It labels High Net Worth ($1MM-$10MM) as "dedicated advice and customizable solutions for complex needs." It reports $0.2T of client balances in the Mass Affluent tier.

Position: providers must engage mass-affluent prospects earlier. Cerulli (published 2026-03-25) says opportunities to engage new clients drop from 44% among the affluent under 30 to 24% among those in their 50s. 32% of affluent respondents prefer the same provider for investing and banking. Cerulli says future prospects will likely have several provider relationships before meeting wealth management minimums, and that providers must define what a premium experience entails.

Position: online and remote meetings are becoming normal. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) reports many people still want their advisor to be local but prefer meetings conducted online. It anticipates further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.

Position: multiple channels funneling into advice. Morgan Stanley's 10-Q (published 2026-08-04) says Wealth Management supports clients through three channels: Advisor-Led, Self-Directed and Workplace. On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-15), its CFO said it is working on a referral model for those without an advice relationship, starting as early as financial education and with 401(k) assets. Schwab's CEO (2Q26 call, published 2026-07-21) said more retail clients seek holistic advice "delivered seamlessly on their terms through a combination of people and increasingly AI-enabled technology."

Edward Jones's own channels and segments (2025 10-K, published 2026-03-13): the firm says its branch model is designed to serve clients through deep, personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning, with advisors located in the communities where clients live and work. It also describes a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, and a Workplace initiative.

Position: broader access to products once limited to wealthier clients. Capgemini (published 2026-06-03) expects new fund structures, strategic partnerships and tokenized delivery to lower barriers. It says portfolio construction that once required very substantial minimum investments will become broadly accessible.

gaps.what: No firm discloses quantified adoption of virtual or remote advice delivery. The evidence on remote advice is survey-based (Wealthtender), not firm-reported.

gaps.suggested_source: Industry studies with longitudinal fee and delivery-model data (for example PriceMetrix, Cerulli) and firm filings over time

claims.text: AI in advice delivery - Edward Jones: not found in the evidence provided. The Edward Jones filings in the evidence describe AI only as an industry and competitive development, not as something the firm uses in advice delivery.

AI in advice delivery - Bank of America (Merrill's parent): On the 2Q25 earnings call (July 2025), CEO Brian Moynihan said that in wealth management and other relationship-manager businesses AI is helping relationship managers and advisors search and summarize information, preparing them to deliver personalized planning and pitches to clients, and that copilots help organize prospecting. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), the CFO said the GWIM segment (Merrill plus the Private Bank) benefited from new AI-enabled tools that help advisers prepare for client conversations, identify opportunities and deliver more personalized advice at scale.
claims.source_label: BAC transcript 2025-06-30 [IR]; BAC transcript - GWIM segment 2026-06-30 [IR]

claims.text: AI in advice delivery - Morgan Stanley: On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), the CFO cited early AI use cases, some live and some in pilot, including LeadIQ, an AI-powered lead distribution platform that matches workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitates engagement with financial advisors. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), CEO Ted Pick said the firm's growth plans embed increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside its client base.

AI in advice delivery - Raymond James: On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), CEO Paul Shoukry said the firm rolled out a solution called Ray that advisers and sales assistants use to sift through information and find answers to complicated questions, piloted with a few hundred advisers. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), he said the enterprise rollout of the proprietary AI assistant Raimond was completed, giving staff a secure, plain-language way to access institutional knowledge. The June 2025 investor-day deck lists AI pipeline items including client portfolio analyses and meeting and CRM notes management.
claims.source_label: RJF transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]; RJF deck 2025-06-05, p.98 [IR]

claims.text: AI in advice delivery - Schwab: On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), CEO Rick Wurster said AI can help create personalized, deeper relationships with clients the firm cannot serve at scale one-to-one, and described Portfolio Insights, an AI-enabled experience giving clients tailored insights on their portfolios. Schwab's 3Q26 release (October 2026) lists the launch of Charley, an AI-powered assistant giving U.S. retail clients conversational access to Schwab's tools, and a partnership with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs Schwab serves. Schwab's 2Q26 release (July 2026) describes Portfolio Insights as a generative AI feature that is not investment advice and may be inaccurate.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; SCHW press 2026-09-30 [filing]; SCHW press 2026-06-30 [filing]

claims.text: Productivity and capacity - Edward Jones: not found in the evidence provided. The 10-Qs attribute higher communications and data processing expense to investments in new tools and technology, but do not tie it to AI or to advisor productivity.

Productivity and capacity - Bank of America (Merrill's parent): On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Moynihan said 17,000 programmers use AI coding technology, saving 10-15% in code generation costs, and that the bank is beginning to see AI aiding efficiency. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), he said the tools are designed to help customer relationship managers prepare more thoroughly for client meetings, and the CFO said AI-enabled tools are more embedded in workflows, including client-facing teams, reducing manual work.

Productivity and capacity - Morgan Stanley: advisor-specific productivity or meeting-preparation claims are not found in the evidence provided. Management's statements are enterprise-wide: on the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Pick said firms will spend several points running on being more efficient, and that over time more productive, with AI.

Productivity and capacity - Raymond James: The June 2025 investor-day deck lists Zoom AI Meeting Summaries and GenAI search among advisor tools, and an AI framework goal to integrate AI tools into the advisor platform to reduce administrative workload. In April 2026 Shoukry said the firm is increasing AI integration to improve efficiency and give professionals more time for clients. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026) he said savings of advisers' administrative time let them spend more time on relationships, adding that the firm tells advisers "AI will not replace advisers. Advisers who use AI will replace advisers who do not use AI."
claims.source_label: RJF deck 2025-06-05, p.98 [IR]; RJF deck 2025-06-05, p.96 [IR]; RJF press 2026-03-31 [filing]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]

claims.text: Productivity and capacity - Schwab: On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Wurster described a tool that summarizes past client interactions before a meeting, records the meeting and prepares an action-based summary, which he said the firm believes will make financial consultants more productive and able to serve more clients. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026) he said developer team productivity improved 15% to 20% over the past year; on the 3Q26 call (October 2026) he said about 25%.
claims.source_label: SCHW transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; SCHW transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]; SCHW transcript 2026-09-30 [IR]

claims.text: Quantified claims - Edward Jones: no AI-specific results, adoption or investment figures are found in the evidence provided.

Quantified claims - Bank of America (Merrill's parent): On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Moynihan said more than 200,000 teammates are using AI-enabled capabilities, generating more than 400,000 prompts a day, with over 300 AI use cases approved, all with good economics, 114 live generative AI use cases and 34 fully implemented. The 3Q26 release (October 2026) says that with more than 200,000 teammates using AI tools and 300-plus approved use cases, "we are turning our scale into a competitive advantage." The November 2025 investor-day deck states 100% of Private Bank teammates have access to AI tools. These figures are enterprise-wide, not Merrill-only.
claims.source_label: BAC transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]; BAC press 2026-09-30 [filing]; BAC deck 2025-11-05, p.37 [IR]

claims.text: Quantified claims - Morgan Stanley: no AI-specific figures are found in the evidence provided. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), Pick said confidence in the efficiency and effectiveness potential of AI-related technologies increases each quarter, and on the 3Q26 call (October 2026) the CFO said AI-related technology investments position the firm to strengthen its competitive moats.

Quantified claims - Raymond James: The October 2025 release says the firm made significant investments of approximately $1 billion in technology including AI during the fiscal year and created the roles of Chief AI Officer and Head of AI Strategy. On the 1Q26 and 2Q26 calls (April and July 2026), Shoukry cited $1.1 billion spent on technology (and AI), said AI will differentiate firms, and that smaller firms cannot keep up with that level of investment.
claims.source_label: RJF press 2025-09-30 [filing]; RJF transcript 2026-03-31 [IR]; RJF transcript 2026-06-30 [IR]

claims.text: Quantified claims - Schwab: On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Wurster said every one of the firm's 33,000 employees has AI tools. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), he said developer productivity is up about 25%, that 77% of U.S. investors use AI while more than 90% prefer human involvement alongside it, and that the combination of people, technology, scale and value is a powerful advantage that is very difficult to replicate.

Overall - who claims the most: the quantified claims are on different metrics: use cases, prompts and live deployments at Bank of America; technology dollars at Raymond James; developer-productivity percentages and employee tool access at Schwab. The evidence does not support a like-for-like ranking, and Edward Jones and Morgan Stanley make no comparable AI-specific figures in the evidence.

claims.text: Future of advice and risks - Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (published March 2026) states that the industry is seeing more firms use artificial intelligence technologies and lower-cost computer-based "robo-advice", which has required and is expected to require significant investments, and that the firm competes with robo-advisors and lower-cost options. It says use of AI by the firm or its third parties may expose it to additional information-security and legal risk, increased regulation and regulatory scrutiny, and reputational harm, and lists AI among the strategic risks it addresses through its initiatives.

Future of advice and risks - Bank of America (Merrill's parent): On the 3Q25 call (October 2025), Moynihan said the bank's view of AI is "enhanced intelligence, not an artificial intelligence" and that teammates remain critical to delivering services. The 2025 10-K (published February 2026) says expanded AI use, including autonomous AI agents, may increase data risk, control failures and operational, legal and regulatory risk, and that AI-related laws and regulations are rapidly evolving.

Future of advice and risks - Morgan Stanley: On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Pick said the continuous "arms race of one AI platform versus another" is additive to the firm's technology, and that the best trusted advisers sitting with the client are "the secret sauce", including the wealth management financial adviser. The 2025 10-K (published February 2026) says the firm's ability to compete across advisor-led, workplace and digital direct channels is affected by its technology supporting client needs, including generative AI.

Future of advice and risks - Raymond James: On the 1Q25 call (April 2025), Shoukry said leadership has conviction that AI will be a game changer but it is still too early to know how it will play out. The 2025 10-K (published November 2025) warns that inaccurate or biased AI output, privacy and security risks and new AI regulation could harm the business and add cost, and notes state and EU AI rules. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), he said the firm tells advisers AI will not replace advisers, and that investment requirements make the industry moat increase.

claims.text: Future of advice and risks - Schwab: On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Wurster said 77% of U.S. investors use AI today while more than 90% prefer human involvement alongside it, that relationships and trust still matter, and that AI has to be safe and secure; he said the firm is blocking unauthorized agents that try to log in on behalf of clients. The July 2026 release cautions that generative AI output may be inaccurate.

claims.text: Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, Feb 2025): McKinsey says that after fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, citing PriceMetrix by McKinsey. Fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.

Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, April 2026): McKinsey writes that it expects repricing of services where clients perceive no differentiation, such as basic tax projections. It calls the fear of an immediate, industry-wide fee freefall "likely overstated" because planning is usually embedded in a broader advisory fee. It believes fee pressure will manifest as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, April 2026): The same piece ties pricing transparency and unbundling directly to the expected form of fee pressure.

Position - asset-based (AUM) fees remain the core model (survey research): The Kitces wellbeing study (published 2023-12-20) found 79% of responding advisor teams primarily derive client revenue from AUM fees. Another 10% were retainer-oriented, and the remainder were divided largely between hourly fees and commissions. Cerulli (published 2025-05-28) found 33% of affluent investors say they compensate their provider via an asset-based fee and 36% prefer it. It also found 21% use a no-fee platform and 20% a commission-based method. Cerulli's analyst says firms should not limit themselves to one engagement option.

Position - asset-based (AUM) fees remain the core model (firm filings): The Bank of America 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says asset management fees are earned as a percentage of client AUM and generally range from 50 bps to 150 bps. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) reports advisory programs AUC of $1.1 trillion, with advisory programs' average AUC up 19%. It attributes its net revenue growth primarily to asset-based fee revenue and "the continued increase in investment of client dollars in advisory programs". On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CFO said a little bit over 20% of adviser-led flows are fee-based flows, and that this "still holds, if not growing".

Position - some rate compression visible from asset mix: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management 10-Q for the period ended 2026-06-30 (published August 2026) says asset management and related fees rose 6% in the quarter and 4% for the year-to-date period. It attributes this to higher average AUM and positive long-term net flows, "partially offset by lower average fee rates, reflecting a change in asset mix".

Position - flat, hourly and tiered alternatives sit alongside AUM pricing in firm disclosures: Raymond James's Wealth Advisory Services brochure (published 2026-09-14) says planning fees can be an hourly rate or fixed (flat) dollar fee. Investment consulting can be an hourly rate, a flat dollar fee, or a percentage of assets under advisement. Hourly fees are generally up to $400 per hour, and a percentage fee is not to exceed an annual rate of 2.25%. Morgan Stanley's advisory brochure (published 2026-11-04) states a wrap fee with a maximum annual asset-based Advisory Fee of 2.0%, plus SMA Sub-Manager Fees that generally range from 0.20% to 0.75%. Edward Jones's Advisory Solutions Fund Models fee (brochure published 2026-03-27) is asset-based, comprising a Program Fee and a Platform Fee, with higher-value accounts generally paying lower rates.
claims.source_label: RJF adv 2026-09-14, p.7 [filing]; MS adv 2026-11-04, p.22 [filing]; EDJ adv 2026-03-27, p.10 [filing]

claims.text: Position - firms say they would adapt pricing if clients move (management statements): On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Raymond James's CEO said the firm wants a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure". He said that if pricing evolves in the industry based on competitive pressures and client preferences, the firm would be "flexible and open to evolving", and that it reviews all pricing, fees and payout on an ongoing basis. On the same call, Schwab's CFO said Schwab's model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service. He added that if those preferences change, Schwab has a lot of flexibility.

Position - fee pressure is driven by competition and low-cost providers (firm risk factors): Edward Jones's 2025 10-K lists competition from robo-advisors and other lower-cost options, from firms offering discount services, and from major competitors that offer zero commissions on stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products. Bank of America's 2025 10-K cites pressure to provide products "on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies". It also cites competitors offering electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, which it says could cause pricing pressure. Morgan Stanley's 2025 10-K says it has experienced and may continue to experience pricing pressures as competitors reduce prices and fees or eliminate commissions. Schwab's 2025 10-K says it monitors pricing against competitors and periodically adjusts advisory fees, mutual fund and ETF expense ratios and commissions, and that reduced commissions or expense ratios could affect results.

Position - client demand for value, not lowest price (surveys and research): McKinsey (Feb 2025) reports that almost 80 percent of affluent households surveyed would rather pay a premium of 50 basis points or more for human advice than use a customized digital service priced at about ten basis points. It also reports that 29 percent are willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) says pricing is the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection but argues this is about demonstrating value for fees, not being cheapest.

Position - AI could compress fees on commoditized planning work (consultancy views, 2026): Deloitte (2026-05-20) says lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, while competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare. McKinsey (2026-04-08) describes markets questioning what clients pay for when AI makes once-invisible work fast and cheap. McKinsey says the advantage shifts toward firms that can prove and monetize outcomes. This sits alongside McKinsey's view that blanket fee cuts are unlikely.
claims.source_label: Research research 2026-05-20 [research]; Research research 2026-04-08, p.6 [research]; Research research 2026-04-08, p.3 [research]

claims.text: Position - price transparency has itself driven competition (Raymond James): Raymond James's FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says that in fixed income and equity markets regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins. The firm says it believes pricing pressures will continue as some competitors seek market share by reducing fees, commissions or margins.

Position - transparency is delivered mainly through disclosure and conflict documentation (firm brochures): Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30, September 18, 2026 update) adds disclosure of new Support Fees, which it describes as a type of revenue sharing. It expects to begin receiving them on January 1, 2027, from third-party firms. It also adds disclosure of optional Data Analytics services and associated conflicts of interest. Merrill says it addresses compensation conflicts through brochure disclosure and by requiring advisors to recommend products that are in clients' best interest "considering cost". Schwab's brochure (published 2026-10-15) says its advisory fee may cost more or less than paying separately and that some reports show performance net of the fee while others show it gross. Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) says fund fees and expenses are embedded in the fund price and are not included in the Fee amount shown in account statements.
claims.source_label: MER adv 2026-10-30, p.2 [filing]; MER adv 2026-10-30, p.54 [filing]; SCHW adv 2026-10-15, p.7 [filing]; MS adv 2026-11-04, p.26 [filing]

claims.text: Regulatory enforcement on hidden or unfair charges (disclosed events): Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) describes a May 12, 2020 SEC settlement order. The SEC found that, from at least October 2012 through June 2017, MSWM gave incomplete and inaccurate information in wrap fee program communications. As a result, some clients paid transaction-based charges that were not visible to them. A trade-press item (published 2026-10-16) reports a NASAA-led settlement over minimum commission practices. It says firms must certify that commission policies and supervisory procedures were revised to ensure charges are fair and reasonable. It lists earlier NASAA-led settlements with Raymond James (July 2023, $13 million) and with Edward Jones and others (June 2025, $9.3 million).
claims.source_label: MS adv 2026-11-04, p.38 [filing]; MER trade 2026-10-16 [trade press (indicative only)]

claims.text: Regulatory framework referenced: A FINRA oversight document (published 2025-12-09) lists SEC staff guidance on Regulation Best Interest observations, conflicts of interest, account recommendations, and Form CRS disclosures. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K says it operates in a regulatory environment with ongoing change and that legislative and regulatory initiatives could affect how it markets products and interacts with clients.

Position - investors still do not clearly understand what they pay (FINRA Foundation, published 2025-12-04): Respondents most often mention account service fees (44 percent) and fees or commissions on trades (41 percent) as fees they pay. Of mutual fund or ETF owners, 45 percent report paying fund fees, 41 percent say they do not, and 13 percent do not know. In total, 20 percent of respondents do not think they pay fees of any kind and 18 percent do not know how much they pay. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) separately reports that 73% of participants consider fee transparency the most important trust factor.

Position - platform-level 'support' and data fees are being added or extended (Merrill): Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30) says Support Fees apply to third-party mutual funds, actively-managed ETFs and certain annuities, and to Style Manager Strategies. For actively-managed ETFs, Support Fees will be up to 0.10% annually of fund assets held in client accounts in the program. For annuities, they will be up to 0.15% on contract purchases. Merrill says Support Fees are a type of revenue sharing. Data Analytics fees are typically $125,000 to $860,000 per year, and $25,000 to $550,000 per year for passively-managed ETF data. Merrill also states it will charge the Support Fee only on underlying investments, so the same assets are not subject to more than one Support Fee.
claims.source_label: MER adv 2026-10-30, p.2 [filing]; MER adv 2026-10-30, p.60 [filing]

claims.text: Position - platform-level 'support' and data fees are being added or extended (Schwab): Schwab's investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) states that "New servicing fees will provide meaningful portion of ETF economics" and that discussions are already underway. Schwab's 10-K (published 2026-02-25) describes mutual fund and ETF service fees charged for services to Schwab and third-party funds, and order flow revenue from trade execution venues.

Position - platform-level fees are linked to zero commissions (trade-press attribution, Merrill coverage 2026-09-29): Trade press quotes sources saying the platform tolls at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions. It quotes consultant Greg O'Gara saying Merrill's disclosure acknowledges that support fees can limit the range of products available to clients. It also quotes the firm as saying it will have a financial incentive to make available and recommend products from third-party firms that pay fees for data analytics. Trade press reports Wells Fargo, UBS and Morgan Stanley charge their own data analytics fees.

Position - the debate over cash-sweep economics versus explicit fees is live: In the 1Q26 call (April 2026) a Wolfe Research analyst asked Raymond James whether it would consider platform fees if competitors pivot to a more fee-based model to reduce reliance on cash economics. Raymond James's FY2025 10-K and its fiscal Q2 2025 10-Q (August 2025) say its PCG results depend on how client cash is allocated across RJBDP, CIP and ESP. The 10-Q also says RJBDP fees decreased on a lower average third-party bank yield. Schwab's CFO said on the 1Q26 call that client cash is actively allocated, with transactional cash at about 4% of client assets. Merrill's brochure says there is no charge or fee for participation in its Cash Sweep Program and that advisors receive no additional compensation for sweep assets. Morgan Stanley's brochure says its Sweep Banks' lending and investing income is greater than fees earned from managing and distributing sweep-eligible money market funds.

claims.text: Edward Jones's own product-level fee structure (brochure and 10-K): Edward Jones's Advisory Solutions Fund Models account pays an asset-based fee comprising a Program Fee and a Platform Fee. ETFs, affiliated and unaffiliated mutual funds in the account also carry internal fees and expenses described in each fund's prospectus. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K says other asset-based fee revenue consists of revenue sharing, fund adviser fees, cash solutions and Trust Co. fees.

adjacent.text: Trade press (Merrill coverage, published 2026-09-29) says that, per its sources, fee-based program fees at Merrill are comparable to RIA pricing at 1.00% and 1.40% of assets typically, and as high as 1.75%. adjacent.text: Raymond James reports an average fee rate of 0.36% on $123.3 billion of total financial assets under management at June 30, 2026 (equity 0.58%, fixed income 0.29%, balanced 0.35%).

gaps.what: Evidence on the adoption of subscription or retainer fee models beyond one 2023 survey (10% of teams retainer-oriented). The evidence shows no time series, no firm disclosure of subscription pricing, and nothing showing a shift in the mix of AUM, flat, hourly and subscription fees.

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) lists "changing client demographics, preferences and values" and "changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs" among the factors that may adversely affect the Partnership's ability to compete and adapt its business model, alongside generational wealth transfer. The filing does not break these preferences out by age.

A BofA Private Bank study (published 2024-06-18) of wealthy Americans reports that 72% of younger investors (ages 21-43) believe above-average returns are no longer possible from traditional stocks and bonds alone, against 28% of investors over 44. Among younger high-net-worth investors, 47% of portfolios are in stocks and bonds versus 74% for older investors, and 17% are in alternatives versus 5%. 93% plan to allocate more to alternatives, and 49% own crypto. This is a wealthy-investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.

The FINRA Foundation investor study (published 2025-12-04) finds investors aged 18-34 much more likely to own individual stocks than mutual funds (82% vs 47%). It also finds them much more likely than older investors to have an options account and to have traded options. Half or more of those under 35 say they invest for social responsibility, entertainment and social activity reasons, though enthusiasm for these has declined noticeably relative to 2021. This is a general US investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.
claims.source_label: Research research 2025-12-04, p.10 [research]; Research research 2025-12-04, p.22 [research]

claims.text: A BofA Private Bank study (published 2026-06-17) defines younger investors as Gen Z and Millennials aged 21 to 45. It reports that 67% believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns. Younger investors allocate more to alternatives (15%) and crypto (13%) than older investors, and 88% say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years. This is a wealthy-investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the Partnership is investing in initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs. These include recently launched Financial Planning Services, where clients get a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities. The 10-K also lists targeted client initiatives: High Net Worth, Workplace, and "a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors." The filing says it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives and that their success depends on broad adoption by advisors, CSTPs and home office associates.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes the existing offering as investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings, delivered through branch teams. Its Digital and Data division is described as providing new tools so branch teams can hold deeper discovery conversations and give more comprehensive advice and planning.
